submission.natural_language_explanation: Induction head: it fires on a GPT-2 token inside the second (or later) occurrence of a multi-token span that already appeared earlier in the context, i.e. when the current token and the one or more tokens immediately before it reproduce an earlier sequence, and it attends to the token that followed the earlier copy. Strength grows with the length of the matched run (about 0.1-0.3 of max after 1-2 matched tokens, 0.5-0.9 after 3+ matched tokens, regardless of distance back), and it stays near its floor (~0.05 of max) on first occurrences, on novel text, and on isolated repeats of common function-word bigrams such as ' on the'.

Pscp utility allows you to transfer/copy files to multiple remote Linux servers using single terminal with one single command, this tool is a part of Pssh (Parallel SSH Tools), which provides parallel versions of OpenSSH and other similar tools such as:

pscp – is utility for copying files in parallel to a number of hosts. prsync – is a utility for efficiently copying files to multiple hosts in parallel. pnuke – it helps to kills processes on multiple remote hosts in parallel. pslurp – it helps to copy files from multiple remote hosts to a central host in parallel.

When working in a network environment where there are multiple hosts on the network, a System Administrator may find these tools listed above very useful.

In this article, we shall look at some useful examples of Pscp utility to transfer/copy files to multiple Linux hosts on a network.

To use the pscp tool, you need to install the PSSH utility on your Linux system, for installation of PSSH you can read this article.

Almost all the different options used with these tools are the same except for few that are related to the specific functionality of a given utility.

How to Use Pscp to Transfer/Copy Files to Multiple Linux Servers

While using pscp you need to create a separate file that includes the number of Linux server IP address and SSH port number that you need to connect to the server.

Copy Files to Multiple Linux Servers

Let’s create a new file called “myscphosts.txt” and add the list of Linux hosts IP address and SSH port (default 22) number as shown.

192.168.0.3:22 192.168.0.9:22

Once you’ve added hosts to the file, it’s time to copy files from local machine to multiple Linux hosts under /tmp directory with the help of following command.

# pscp -h myscphosts.txt -l tecmint -Av wine-1.7.55.tar.bz2 /tmp/ OR # pscp.pssh -h myscphosts.txt -l tecmint -Av wine-1.7.55.tar.bz2 /tmp/

On the northern edge of the county, where the river bends sharply around a low hill, sits the small harbor town of Aldervik. For most of the year the population stays under four hundred, mostly families who have worked the water for generations. The harbor itself is shallow, sheltered by a granite breakwater built in the 1890s after a winter storm wrecked three fishing boats in a single night. Visitors arriving by road pass first through a corridor of wind-bent pines, then over a single-lane bridge whose iron rails have been repainted so often that the bolts no longer sit flush against the wood. The main street runs from the bridge to the quay, lined with sheds, a cooperative store, and a bakery that opens at half past five. In summer the bakery sells cardamom buns to tourists who queue along the pavement, and in winter it sells almost nothing but rye bread to the same twelve customers.

The council meets on the first Thursday of each month in a room above the cooperative store. Minutes are kept by hand in a ledger that goes back to 1947, and the clerk has a habit of reading the previous month's decisions aloud before any new business is raised. Most meetings last less than an hour. Arguments tend to be about mooring fees, the cost of dredging, and whether the streetlights should stay on past midnight in July, when the sky never quite goes dark.

Fishing remains the backbone of the economy, though the fleet is smaller than it once was. Six boats work out of the harbor, landing chiefly mackerel and crab, with a few boxes of scallops when the weather allows. The fish house on the quay handles the catch, and its proprietor, who took over from her father in 2011, has lately been experimenting with direct sales to restaurants inland. She drives the boxes herself on Tuesdays, leaving before dawn and returning in the afternoon, and she says the margins are better but the hours are worse.

Tourism has grown slowly and unevenly. A guesthouse opened in the old schoolhouse in 2016, and a second followed three years later in a converted boathouse. Neither is large. The council resisted a proposal for a marina, partly on cost grounds and partly because the fishermen feared the moorings would be priced beyond their reach. The compromise, approved after two years of argument, was a small pontoon for visiting yachts, with fees set high enough to keep demand modest.

Every visitor stops to photograph the brass clock above the harbor office. The clock has not worked since the spring of 2009, when a power cut burned out its motor, and the council has twice voted to repair it without ever finding the money. Even the locals still photograph the brass clock above the harbor office at noon, out of habit more than affection, while the gulls wheel over the quay and the ferry sounds its horn across the water.
